/Through Tuesday/...
Issued at 258 PM MDT Tue Oct 20 2026

Recent radar imagery shows a couple of showers moving off the 
northern CO foothills. These showers are being supported by 
enhanced vorticity and lift from the weak shortwave moving across 
northern CO this afternoon. Temperatures are sitting in the 60s to
70s over the Denver metro and plains, with 50s and low 60s across
the mountains. Isolated showers will continue to be possible over
the high terrain through sunset, although very minimal rainfall 
(perhaps just a few hundredths) is expected to reach the ground. 
Skies will be mostly clear tonight with morning lows expected to 
be slightly warmer than this morning over the plains, with 
temperatures in the low 50s for the Denver metro, and some mid 40s
in the usual cold spots out in the northeast CO plains.

An upper level ridge will begin to build over the area tonight, 
reinforcing above-average temperatures for the rest of the work week 
as temperatures soar into the mid to upper 70s at low elevations. 
This upper level ridge will also strengthen southwest flow aloft and 
bring an increase in Pacific moisture later in the day ahead of a 
strong cutoff low to the west. However, we do not expect any rain 
chances to arrive to the mountains of our area until the late 
afternoon/early evening. Moisture transport will intensify late 
Wednesday night as the cutoff low reaches the California coast, and 
a robust subtropical jet channels Pacific moisture towards the Four 
Corners in an atmospheric river-like fashion. A first round of 
isolated showers will be possible into the overnight hours over the 
mountains, and mid level clouds will begin to drift over the plains. 

Shower coverage should increase over the high terrain Thursday 
afternoon. However, as has been outlined in previous AFDs, 
southwesterly flow aloft and limited instability will favor more 
modest rainfall amounts for southwest CO, with much lighter amounts 
over our CWA. Recent model trends have showed little change in QPF for
the central mountains and Front Range, with amounts generally 
ranging from a trace up to 0.50", and perhaps some locally higher
amounts for the mountains of Park County. Given the tropical 
nature of this airmass, it will be difficult to get snow 
accumulation out of this system, with perhaps only some dustings 
above 12,000 ft. For the Denver metro, a few sprinkles up to a 
trace of rainfall cannot be ruled out Thursday afternoon if any 
showers are able to survive off the foothills. Otherwise, it will 
be another warm day for the plains, with temperatures in the mid 
70s and partly cloudy skies. 

The cutoff low will begin to weaken late Thursday into Friday as the 
trough axis drifts over Utah. However, a tight pressure gradient 
will encourage breezy south-southwest winds over the east CO plains 
throughout the day on Friday. Current model guidance suggests wind 
gusts up to 30-40 mph possible over a large portion of the east CO 
plains. We also expect temperatures to climb into the upper 70s with 
clearing skies, warm air advection, and weak downsloping, 
potentially leading to a slight drop in humidities (20%-30%). If 
humidities trend any drier, we could be looking at critical fire 
weather conditions Friday afternoon over portions of the 
CO plains given the overlap of gusty winds and drier air. 

A cold front will push through the area Saturday morning, bringing 
another period of northerly breezy winds with gusts up to 25-30 mph. 
There is still some model disagreement regarding the strength, 
and the moisture accompanying this front. Some ensemble members 
suggest a moister and cooler scenario, with low clouds and 
afternoon temperatures over the Denver metro dipping well below 
average. Other model solutions hint at partly sunny skies and 
temperatures in the low 60s, which is right at the climatological 
average. It is worth noting, however, that models have trended a 
bit moister with the front since yesterday, with some light 
mountain snow accumulations becoming increasingly likely Saturday 
into Sunday. Looking ahead, there is considerable spread in 
synoptic ensemble guidance, making next week's forecast quite 
uncertain at this time.
